title: How Mature Is Your Team?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that team maturity is a different kind of operation, not just a smoother version of the same team. Mature teams talk openly about mistakes, and a hospital-unit study found they reported more errors, not fewer, because they were willing to raise them. They lean into disagreement, arguing hard about the work without making it personal, and so reach consensus on difficult decisions faster. They coordinate with little effort because members know who knows what, and they spend time up front on root causes and schedule midpoint reviews. They also seek outside voices, since cohesion that shuts out other views is the start of decay. The note adds that time alone does not produce maturity, and that it starts with a leader who prizes candor over comfort.
points: Mature teams surface and discuss their mistakes openly, which is why hospital units with mature teams reported more errors, not fewer.
They treat disagreement as healthy, arguing about the work without making it personal, and usually decide difficult matters faster.
Members keep an accurate map of who knows what and defer to the person with the most expertise.
Mature teams invest time in root causes, schedule midpoint reviews and welcome outside challenge rather than closing ranks.
Maturity does not come with tenure; it starts with a self-confident leader who privileges candor over comfort and shares leadership.
quotes: Most notably, mature teams are willing to talk about their mistakes. In fact, in a study of hospital units, mature teams reported more medical errors, not fewer.
Mature teams don’t avoid conflict. Instead, they lean into it, arguing harder about the work while keeping the arguments from becoming personal.
As a consequence, they usually reach consensus on difficult decisions more quickly than other teams and stand together behind those decisions when they face criticism.
Mature teams also coordinate with less effort. Members build an accurate map of who knows what and defer to whoever knows the most.
Cohesion that closes a team off from outside views is not maturity. It is the start of decay.
Unfortunately, time alone does not produce maturity. A large majority of teams never reach the mature stage, no matter how long they work together.
It all starts with a leader who privileges candor over comfort and builds the team’s habits around it.
